title: Temperature Scales
notes: A temperature scale is a calibration of a thermometer based on two fixed reference points. The three most common scales in physics are Celsius (°C), Fahrenheit (°F) and Kelvin (K).
Every scale is defined using the freezing point and boiling point of water:

ScaleFreezing pointBoiling point
Celsius0°C100°C
Fahrenheit32°F212°F
Kelvin273.15 K373.15 K

Kelvin is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. It is an absolute scale starting at absolute zero (0 K), the lowest possible temperature where molecular motion theoretically stops. We write 273 K, never °K or degree Kelvin.

summary: Temperature scales are defined using the freezing and boiling points of water. Celsius sets them at 0°C and 100°C, Fahrenheit at 32°F and 212°F, and Kelvin is an absolute scale starting at 0 K. Kelvin is the SI unit and all thermodynamic calculations use it.
examples: Ice cream melts at about −3°C, which is about 26.6°F.
keyPoints: Kelvin is the SI unit of temperature and is an absolute scale.
0 K is absolute zero; Kelvin values are never negative.
A change of 1 K equals a change of 1°C.
Celsius and Fahrenheit read the same value at −40°.
